faqs.answer: An eclipsing binary is a pair of stars orbiting each other such that, from Earth's viewpoint, one star periodically passes in front of the other. During an eclipse, the combined light from the system dims. By measuring these dips in brightness, astronomers can learn about the stars' sizes, orbital periods, and relative properties.
faqs.question: What is an eclipsing binary star?

faqs.answer: A candidate is a target that passed statistical quality checks and was flagged as novel (not already in six known catalogs). A confirmed result is a candidate that also passed Star Vetter's automated pixel-level check, meaning the eclipse signal is verified to come from the target star itself and not from a nearby contaminating source. Confirmation by this pipeline does not mean the candidate is scientifically verified; it means it has passed this project's automated vetting steps.
faqs.question: What is the difference between a 'candidate' and a 'confirmed' result on this site?

faqs.answer: Star Vetter includes a logistic-regression model trained on 1,121 labeled examples. It provides a second opinion on which candidates are likely to pass the pixel-level check, and it outperforms the rule-based baseline pipeline. However, the ML score is not used to decide which candidates get checked or to filter the pipeline; it is intended as additional context only.
faqs.question: What is the machine-learning screening score?

faqs.answer: Each candidate undergoes an automated pixel-level check. This test examines the spatial distribution of light in the TESS images to confirm that the eclipse signal originates from the target star itself, not from a nearby star whose light contaminates the photometry. Candidates that pass this check are listed as confirmed on the site.
faqs.question: How does Star Vetter check whether a candidate is real?

faqs.answer: Star Vetter includes an odd/even eclipse-depth test: it compares the depth of odd-numbered eclipses against the depth of even-numbered eclipses. If these depths differ significantly, the period may be an alias (a harmonic or sub-harmonic of the true period), and that caveat is noted on the candidate's page.
faqs.question: What happens if the orbital period looks aliased?

faqs.answer: Yes. Each confirmed candidate's page includes a link to its TESS light curve data and enough detail (target ID, period, eclipse depths) for you to examine the data yourself using publicly available tools. You can also cross-check against the six catalogs Star Vetter uses: VSX, ASAS-SN, Gaia eclipsing-binary table, Gaia variable classification, the TESS EB catalog, and ExoFOP.
faqs.question: Can I verify a result myself?

faqs.answer: Being listed on this site marks the end of what the Star Vetter pipeline itself does. The site makes no claims about whether a candidate will be studied further, added to other catalogs, or receive follow-up observations. That is beyond the scope of this automated vetting project.
faqs.question: What happens to a candidate after it is listed on Star Vetter?

narrative: Star Vetter automatically vets candidate eclipsing binary stars found in TESS satellite data. The pipeline begins by sampling targets and extracting light curves, applies statistical quality checks, cross-references six known variable-star catalogs to flag novel candidates, and runs an automated pixel-level check to confirm that the eclipse signal comes from the target star itself rather than a nearby contaminant. So far, the project has sampled 7,430 targets (about 0.9% of the survey footprint) and confirmed 116 candidates. A machine-learning model trained on 1,121 labeled examples provides a second opinion on candidate quality, outperforming the baseline rule-based pipeline. These results are trustworthy because they combine automated statistical rigor, explicit cross-matching against existing catalogs, and pixel-level verification--but each candidate's individual page notes any open caveats that remain.
